subject: Prospective PhD applicant (Fall 2027): how people understand apps that act on their data
body:
Dear Professor Li,

I'm applying to the Khoury HCI PhD program for Fall 2027, and I'm writing because your work is close to the questions I want to study.

I've been a product data analyst at a consumer fitness app for four years. One of our features rewrites users' workout plans using their activity, sleep, and heart-rate data. By our metrics, its launch succeeded. In the open-ended survey responses, though, about one in ten people said their plan had changed and they had no idea why, or asked how the app knew they'd slept badly. A few turned off health-data sharing. Later, I took notes for our UX research team's interviews about the feature. What stayed with me was hearing people explain, in their own words, what they thought the app was doing with their data.

I want to understand what people think is going on when an app uses their own data to decide things for them, and what would make them feel they still have a say. Your COLM 2026 paper on autonomy and personalization stood out to me. The finding that handing control back to users improved their sense of control, and reduced the trust costs of personalization, is close to what I want to explore. I'm especially interested in everyday consumer apps that act on personal data without being asked.

I'd be grateful to know whether you expect to take new PhD students for Fall 2027. I'd be happy to share my CV, and I'd welcome the chance to talk briefly if you're open to it.

Best regards,
Riley Nakamura
riley.nakamura@example.com
